Czech Republic Imposes Temporary Tariffs on Imported Transport Equipment, Impacting Logistics Sector

PRAGUE – The Czech government has introduced temporary tariffs on select imported transportation equipment in response to ongoing trade negotiations with external partners, causing immediate disruptions within the country’s transportation and logistics industry.

Under the new measure, which took effect late last week, tariffs of up to 18 percent have been levied on imported buses, rail components, and specialized freight vehicles entering the Czech Republic from outside the European Union. The move is aimed at protecting domestic manufacturers and pressuring foreign suppliers amid what officials describe as “unfair trading practices” by several non-EU countries.

The decision has sent ripples through the Czech transportation and logistics sector, which relies heavily on a combination of domestic production and imported equipment to maintain and expand its fleets. Dopravni Podnik Hlm Prahy AS, the operator of Prague's public transport network, confirmed that the new tariffs have already led to delays and increased costs in its ongoing procurement projects.

“We are in the midst of modernizing our tram and bus fleets. The sudden imposition of these tariffs has complicated our supply chains and increased our expenses significantly,” said Martin Havelka, spokesperson for Dopravni Podnik Hlm Prahy AS. “We are assessing how this will affect our modernization timelines and operational budgets.”

Industry association Česká Unie Logistiky estimated that the tariffs could raise overall costs for logistics firms by 6 to 10 percent in the coming quarter, depending on the mix of imported versus domestically produced equipment. Smaller operators, such as Brno-based TransWay Express, are reportedly facing the toughest challenges, with several projects paused pending further clarification from customs officials.

Government representatives defended the move as necessary. “We are protecting Czech jobs and manufacturing capacity,” said Deputy Minister for Trade Petra Vondrová. “We regret any short-term inconvenience, but our long-term objective is to secure fairer terms for Czech companies in the global market.”

The Czech Chamber of Transport expressed concern about the timing and scope of the measure. In a statement, the chamber urged policymakers to “ensure that any trade defense instrument does not unduly disrupt the efficiency and reliability of the country’s transport and logistics operations.”

As the tariffs remain in force, industry stakeholders are closely monitoring the situation and urging swift resolution of the underlying trade dispute. For now, logistics companies across the Czech Republic are recalculating their budgets and re-evaluating their procurement strategies, as the sector adapts to a new and uncertain trading environment.
